The Weekly Register
LOCAL MATTERS.
It was a disgraceful day of rioting and drunkenness. Such a day has never before been witnessed in Point Pleasant, and we hope its likes will never be seen again.

Early in the morning a lot of worthless whites and worthless negroes began drinking, and by nine o'clock a very considerable number of them were beastly drunk and disorderly, and cursing and quarreling between themselves. Soon they began to insult and assault decent people as they passed along the streets. Officers were resisted, cursed and threatened, when attempting to enforce the law.

All day hundreds of people were upon the streets, and the town kept in a feverish state of excitement, because every moment, it was expected a bloody riot would occur.

Great crowds of excited whites and blacks were gathered at different points on Main street; some of whom were wanting to fight, urging and threatening a riot, and revolvers and knives were whipped out to deal death and destruction to all who opposed them should a conflict occur. Some were there to keep the peace and pacify the drunken roughs and rowdies, of both colors, knowing full well that if a knock down was permitted, or a shot fired, it would plunge the town into a fearful riot, resulting in a war of races; and would draw into it all the better class of our citizens, both white and black, as a matter of self-preservation and protection to their families.

Some of the colored people were threatening to clean out the whites and take the town, and some of the whites were threatening to clean out the negroes and drive them from the town. These threats came from the lower order of whites and blacks, and had no sanction or encourage from the better disposed citizens of either color.

As we said before, a riot was looked for momentarily, and men began to prepare for any emergency. Arms and ammunition were made ready, and put within easy reach and would have been used with deadly effect upon the roughs had an outbreak occurred.

The most singular thing of all was that not a single rioter was arrested, of either color. Why, we cannot say, unless there was an indisposition to enforce the law on Christmas day, or the officers were powerless. Fully twenty-five men, both whites and negroes, should have been arrested and placed in jail.

The whole proceedings was a disgrace to the town, and the action of its officers, a burlesque upon law and order. We do not believe in leniency to rioter, roughs and rowdies, but in stern and firm dealing with such characters, and meting out severe punishments to them.

We hope now that our Mayor will cause the arrest of all who were engaged in these riotous proceedings, try them, fine them, jail them, and when they are turned out, place them under bonds for their good behavior. We also hope that our next Grand Jury will inquire into this matter, and indict the ring-leaders, who were urging on and instigating a riot and threatening the town. A few years in the Penitentiary may do some of them good.
This is the only way to break up this lawlessness, which has been growing worse and worse for the past year or two.
If severe and rigorous measures are not used to break up this ruffianism, neither life nor property will be safe in this place.
It has now come to such a point that respectable ladies unaccompanied by an escort, cannot come out on the streets, after dark, without being shocked and insulted by the black-guardism of these low roughs and vagabonds.

PERSONALS.—We had a call from Mr. E. C. Harpold, the first of the week. He was just from Texas and gives a glowing account of that far-off State. He has struck a bonanza in the salt business in Texas, and is now arranging to put up a 500 barrel furnace in the great salt basin of Texas. He is here to procure a corps of practical salt-makers, whom he will take back with him this week. He is in high spirits and sees a fortune within his grasp. He has had bad luck in this county, and has been badly treated as well. If he has not the capital of some men, he has the experience in salt making, the push, perseverence and tenacity to succeed in this new venture. He is one of those kind of men that cannot be kept down by adversity. We are glad to chronicle the bright prospects he has before him, and we wish that he may succeed beyond his most sanguine expectations. We regret to lose him and his estimable family, but at the same time we congratulate Vanzant county upon so valuable and respectable an addition to its population.

On Monday we had a very agreeable call from James L. Rice, Esq., of Cooper District. He gave us some advice as regards our legislative duties, all of which we promise to heed. He is an intelligent and well read gentleman.

The News and Courrier has received details of the murder of Mrs. Kennedy, in Clarendon County, and of the subsequent lynching of the three murderers, already briefly reported. When her husband lett, she shut the door and sat down by the window to write a letter to her mother. DOUBLE MURDER.

DAVENPORT, Ia., Dec. 11.—A foul murder, or rather a double murder, was committed this morning three miles from Colona, on the Chicago, Rock Island & Pacific Railroad, thirteen miles east of Davenport. The subjects of the startling crime were Thomas Dilley and his wife. Mr. Dilley is an old resident, and one of the largest farmers in Henry County. The details of the work of butchery can only be known from the results as they were found this morning. Mr. Dilley was dead in his room, his skull having been broken and his head horribly disfigured. In the same room was Mrs. Dilley, entirely unconscious, while her body and head showed the work of heavy blows. It is not expected that she can survive the night. Near by the mangled bodies was an old spade handle heavily stained with blood, and there is little doubt that this in hands of villians was the executioner. Whether the crime was inspired by the hope of treasure or not is unknown. There was quite a sum of money in the house, but it was undisturbed. The more generally-accepted theory is that the murder was the result of an old grudge which had involved several parties in a lawsuit, and which was recently decided in favor of Mr. Dillon. The only property missing is a small silver watch, with the point of the minute-hand broken, and a small gold chain attached, and a large hunting-case watch, nearly new.

Two parties are strongly suspected, and their descriptions have been given to the police. One is known as Clement Gallion, aged about 19 years, weight 170 pounds, six feet tall, dark hair and eyes, large mouth, round chin, and no whiskers. Gallion wore a navy-blue shirt, with the print of a horse shoe on the bosom, and the word "Luck" beneath.

GENESEO, Ill., Dec. 11.—Last Friday John Dilley, a farmer residing near Green River, left Geneseo with the proceeds of the sale of his hogs. About 12 o'clock that night his little girl of 12 years was awakened by a noise, and looking up saw a man in the room. She thought it her father, but later, hearing so much noise, jumped up to see her father shot, the ball passing through his forehead and coming out of the back of his head, instantly killing him, and to see her mother beaten to death with a club. Being frightened, she curled down into bed till all was still. Getting up, she found both parents dead. She dressed the two children,—one 6 years old and the other about 4,—and walked about three-fourths of a mile to give the alarm. Two men who have been husking corn are suspected, but have not been seen since Thursday last.

[Special Dispatch to The News and Courter]

KINGSTREE, Dec. 10.—The hanging was done at 4 p. m. Wednesday within twenty yards of the place of the murder by about one hundred and fifty white men and fifty colored men and women. The two Brandts were employed and lived on the place, and were arrested together, with many others, but were turned loose all, and Barnes was arrested about four miles from the place of murder, where he went immediately after the deed. He was seen to spend money on Monday and known to have none on Saturday. He first denied having anything to do with murder, but afterwards confessed with such minuteness of circumstances as led to the conviction of the two others. The negroes begged the whites to permit them to take the prisoners and burn them alive. This was refused, but a vote taken as to whether they should be jailed and await the court or be lynched. Only twenty-three voted to await the law, and getting halters from the stables near, the murderers were put into a car; and swung from the nearest tree to the spot of their deed that was large enough to support them. Another Appeal to Lynch Law.

Elsewhere in the Press and Banner may be found a detailed account of the murder of a young wife by three negroes, and the speedy lynching of the accused. It seems to us that the offence of murder in this State is on the increase, and we are able to attribute the cause to no other reason than the fact that the crime of murder is so seldom punished, or if punished at all, the penalty imposed is so slight that it amounts to about the same thing as an acquittal. As a rule no white man in South Carolina is ever convicted of murder, while it is a known fact that very few of the negroes who are convicted, suffer at the hands of the law. Through the squamishness of juries and the legal technicalities brought into court nearly every murderer escapes. We hope that we may be pardoned for referring to one or two cases which were recently tried at Walhalla. The Moores were charged with the murder of Brice. The proof was such as to convince nearly everybody except the jury. Another case was that of two men charged with murder in the killing of a woman in her own door. In the testimony it seems that two men rode by a farm house. The dog at the house ran out in the road, barking. One of the men commenced shooting at the dog. The woman came to the door and asked them not to kill it. They replied by shooting her. Death ensued. The perpetrator of the deed was tried in court and found guilty of manslaughter, and sent to the penitentiary for four years. At the same term of court a negro was convicted of stealing a bale of cotton. He was sent to the penitentiary for three years. In Newberry, we believe, a man was acquitted of killing a blind man. It is a fact that many men have been killed in various parts of this State, and that very few men have suffered for their deeds of blood. These facts have almost created a necessity for lynch law. We think in a normal condition of affairs that our safety is in the courts. But when the courts refuse to give protection, the citizen is called upon to protect himself. In our county three most atrocious murders have been committed since 1876. The Harmons, quiet and inoffensive old people, were stain by negroes at night inside of their dwelling. They were lynched on the spot. In 1878 the Franklin, aged and infirm people who never wronged mortal man, were stain in their own house, while at the evening meal. A coroner's jury was summoned. Circumstances pointed to the guilt of certain parties. The community, relying upon the justice of the courts, sent them to prison, one of whom was convicted—the others were liberated. On the convict no punishment beyond imprisonment has been inflicted. We no longer see bloody bodies, with ghastly wounds. They have been put out of sight, and, for two years the slain have been mouldering in premature graves. Time has softened our feelings, and in this instance, our hearts may be improperly moved in sympathy for the living, around whom cluster so many evidences of guilt. The enormity of crime seems to have lost its hideousness and the pleading tongue of the living appear more eloquent than the dumb wounds of the dead. The cries of the criminal are more potent than the demands of that justice which gives us safety in our homes, around the firesides which our own industry has procured. The last murder in this county occurred on the 17th of November last. Mr. William Maddox, an old man, an industrious and thrifty citizen, and an unobtrusive neighbor, at night, after a day's hard work at gathering his crop, was called from his bed by unknown men, and, in the presence of his family, shot to death. As far as we are informed, very little has, as yet, been done by the peace officers of the State in ferreting out the perpetrators of this unprovoked deceed, which in atrocity, is unsurpassed in the annals of crime. The men of the neighborhood, however, have acted nobly in the matter, and have done all that good and true citizens could do. They quit their work, and for days were in search for the murderers. Besides this, when the efforts of her neighbors had failed, the bereaved widow of the deceased offered a large reward for the arrest and conviction of the assassins. In fact, everything that an indignant and injured neighborhood could do, has been done, but they need the aid and services of the professional detectives which the State could and should furnish. We do not know whether the authorities in Columbia have done anything at all in this matter, but we have no doubt that Governor Hagood will do everything in his power to have the guilty parties brought into court. That official has lately been installed into office, the Legislature is in session and a multiplicity of matters, we know, are making demands upon his time at present. But our people may rest assured that he will do his whole duty in the premises, and that no effort on his part will be lacking to bring the guilty parties to justice. This is the only way to prevent our lapsing into a state of barbarism. Without the enforcement of the criminal law, our civilization is a cheat. The sooner our juries look to the safety and protection of the citizen, the sooner crime will diminish.

Three young colored demons, two boys and a girl, aged respectively 15, 16 and 18, murdered Mrs. Ada Kennedy of Clarendon County on the 4th instant in a most brutal and horrible manner. A short while after Mr. Kennedy left home to secure the presence of his mother with his wife during a three days visit to Charleston, these fiends appeared, demanded money and, being refused, brutally attacked Mrs. Kennedy with hoes and finally killed her by cleaving her skull with a hoe. STATE ITEMS.
An eagle that measured six feet four inches from tip to tip was shot recently in Fulton county.

Land on the Columbia pike, near Lancaster, sold a few days ago at $306 and $360 per acre.

At the February election the people of Norristown shall decide whether that place shall be made a city.

Residents of the county seat of Sulivan don't have to go far for deer. A Laporte man shot a fine buck from his window the other day.

Lewis Cooper, of York county, Pa., was crushed to death last week by a tree falling on him.

Charley Ross' father says he has examined over three hundred lost children in his search for his boy, and that he still has detectives employed to find him.

At Johnstown on Monday morning a week Andrew Mullen, aged 10, while playing near the railroad track stepped in front of an express train and was instantly killed.

Two-thirds of the Grand Army posts of the State will attend Garfield's inauguration.

William N'Intyre, aged thirteen, son of a track foreman at Holidaysburg, rolled off a lounge in his father's house on the 13th and fell on the point of a rusty bayonet with which he was playing. The bayonet entered his neck near the right ear, and was forced clean through his neck, emerging just below the left ear. The father drew the bayonet, but there is no present hope of the boy's recovery.

Samuel Way, a prominent and much esteemed citizen of Mount Joy, died on Saturday evening the 11th aged about one hundred years. He was one of a family of twenty one children by two marriages. His father was a slave during the existence of slavery in this State, having been brought to Peunsylvania direct from Guinea.

William Brocious, a well-to-do farmer, living near Clearfield, left home a month ago to go to the mill, and has not since been heard from.

Anna Bender, a girl of feeble intellect, aged 20 left her home at Small's Mills Quincy township, on the 25th ultime, and was not seen again till the 11th, when her skeleton was found in a piece of woods half a mile distant, her flesh having been mostly devoured by hogs, dogs or wild animals. No clue to the cause of her death was found.

The authorities of Duke Centre, McKean county, are after a notorious character named John Fish, who has enticed a number of girls to that place for immoral purposes. A posse went Fish's house to lynch him, but he had fled.

Frank Gallagher, a young man residing in Lower Yoder township, Cambria county, on Monday a week placed half a pound of powder on the stove to dry. The natural result followed but he was not seriously injured.

Mrs. Robert Smith, of Burnside township, Clearfield county, recently visited some relatives in Cherryhill township, Indiana county. She had carefully wrapped up her two months-old child and carried it with her. When she arrived at her destination she was horrified to see that her child was soothered to death.

Man and Wife Murdered and the Perpetrator Lynched.

Allentown (Pa.), December 27th.—Jacob Gogel and wife, residing four miles from Bethlehem, was found dead in bed this morning, their heads nearly severed from their bodies. A bloody ax was found in the apartment, and the walls were splashed with blood. Joseph Snyder, who boarded with the Gogels, was believed to be the murderer. He was caught by an infuriated mob soon after the discovery of the crime, and was hanged to the nearest tree. The Gogels leave three children.

[SECOND DISPATCH.]

Allentown (Pa.), December 27th.—Joseph Snyder, aged 24, the murderer of Jacob and Anna Gogel, near Bethlehem, was found in a neighboring barn under the straw at 9 o'clock this morning. He was immediately taken back to the house of his victims and questioned as to the murder. He was interrogated by Rev. Mr. Brendle of Bethlehem, and at once confessed to having committed the crime, telling his story with great deliberation. He was in love with the oldest daughter of the Gogels, 16 years of age, but was opposed by her parents. He believed that by killing them all opposition would be removed to his suit. He had scarcely confessed before a rope taken from one of the beds was placed around his neck and he was dragged outside the house and hanged to a large chestnut tree. After being suspended twenty minutes his body was cut down by the poor-house authorities and taken to that institution, where it was found that death was caused by strangulation. The officers of the law made a vain endeavor to restrain the fury of the mob, Detective Yak of Bethlehem firing at one of the ringleaders, without effect. Several thousand people visited the scene of the tragedy during the day.

The proverbial blindness of passion was strongly exemplified by that Northampton county crowd of excited men who hung the brutal murderer of the Gogles. He had frequently made improper advances toward Alice, the prepossessing daughter of Mr. Gogle, aged 16. The daughter had complained to her parents of the actions of Snyder, and her father had had several stormy interviews with him, telling him that he must either leave the house or stop at once his disagreeable attentions to his daughter. On Sunday, Snyder remained home in a cheerful mood, joining with the children and two girl friends, who had come from Farmersville, a few miles distant, to spend the night with them, in singing their Christmas anthems, which they were practising for an entertainment in which they were to take part in a few days. CIRCUMSTANTIAL EVIDENCE.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

Bosrox, Dec. 24.—The case of Catherine Driscoll, to-day found guilty of the manslaughter of Mary Credon, is one of the most interesting trials in Massachusetts for some years, as the conviction was made entirely on circumstantial evidence. The trial was a very sad one, the prisoner every day being accompanied by her family of little children, the youngest sitting in her lap in the dock. The victim was three years old, was seen to enter Driscoll's house soon after dinner, April 15, and her body was found on the railroad track early the next morning, her dinner not having digested, and her clothing dry, notwithstanding heavy rain had fallen during the night. Soon after the dinner, Mrs. Credon missed her daughter, and, looking into Mrs. Driscoll's, saw her with a child in her arms, and on her apron considerable blood, which the woman said, on being questioned, came from a cut finger of her child. In Mrs. Driscoll's cellar blood found on the walls and floor proved to be that of a human being mingled with that of fowls and cows. In the ground under the stairs the hood of the murdered child was dug up. Near by there was some grass corresponding with a quantity of grass clasped in the hand of the murdered child. The blood was claimed by the defense to be that of an animal's alone, and the prisoner swore that she did not kill the child, who was a loved playmate of her children.

Judge Lord said that there was no substantial difference between circumstantial and positive evidence, and leaned to the opinion that the woman committed the deed in a sudden fit of passion, without intention or thought.

The sentence will be imposed Monday, and will probably be for twenty years.

BOLD ROBBERY.

LAFAYETTE, Ind., Dec. 24.—One of the most audacious robberies was committed about noon yesterday at Williamsport, Warren County. Two men entered the store of the Messner Bros. at that place, only one of the firm being present. They asked the price of several articles, and finally requested to see some handkerchiefs. About the same time one of the strangers asked for tobacco, and while young Messner was in the act of getting it he was dealt a terrible blow with a sandbag. The men then fastened the door and tried to get into the safe. The outer doors were open, and they secured about $00 in money. They were unable to open the inside doors, and, returning to Messner, who had now become partially conscious, demanded to know the combination. He refused to give it, when they beat him nearly to death, and then left the store by the rear door. The Town Marshal happened along about that time, and finding the front door locked and seeing a man lying on the floor, forced his way in, releasing Messner and giving an alarm. A large crowd was soon on the hunt, aided by an accurate description of the villains, but they could not be found.

DETROIT, Mich., Dec. 23.—Rev. Samuel B. Carpenter, an Episcopal clergyman of Toledo, recently of this city, was the victim of an audacious robbery on a Lake Shore train last night. As the cars were about to stop at Monroe, a gentlemanly-appearing man inquired the time. As Mr. Carpenter took out his watch it was grabbed by the thief, at the same time other confederates seizing the victim lent him back over the seat and hurriedly riffed his pockets, securing $80, and jumped from the cars before the remaining passengers had time to recover from their astonishment over the affair. St. Louis, Mo., Dec. 25.—About half past 6 this evening, a party of six or eight drunken roughs attempted to enter Swain's keno rooms on Sixth street, between Market and Chestnut, but were refused admittance by Larry O'Brien, the doorkeeper. The roughs immediately became very abusive and quarrelsome, and Joseph O'Brien, a brother of the doorkeeper; James McCormick, Joe Davies and James Kelly, who were standing on the sidewalk, took sides with the doorkeeper. [From The Kanawha Gazette.]
Letter From The Swiss Colony.
Having been requested by you to write on our colonization interests for your valuable paper, I submit the following facts, and trust that our West Virginia papers will be as ready to vindicate the interests of the State, as outsiders and even some who reside in the Valley, are to traduce her and her people.

We have just seen a copy of the Berner Post, published at Bern, Switzerland, in which was produced an article taken from the New Yorker Staats Zeitung, (the largest and most influential German paper published in America), under date of July 12, 1880. The Staats Zeitung claims to have taken the article from the Anziger des Westes, published at St. Louis.

The article in question is an infamous attack against Swiss settling in West Virginia, saying: That lands are unproductive, &c.; that no person could make a living from the soil; that the people were a set of "poor white trash," thieves and cut throats; that innocent settlers were charged $7 to $10 for unimproved lands, &c. The article is interspersed with glowing accounts of the West. The most miserable charge was as follows: "That there was only one Swiss family in the Kanawha Valley, located in a section known as Loup Creek; that the family was shamefully treated; the husband lynched because he allowed his wife to work." You can readily see what effect such articles must have, not only in this country but also abroad.

We have letters to show that in New York there is a regularly organized movement to divert people from coming here. We have also evidence that hardly do the immigrants leave the steamer before they are questioned if they are going South or not. If so, everything that can be is done to keep them back.—We have letters to prove that people who desired to come here were told by ministers of the gospel not to come to West Virginia; that their lives would not be safe; that they would be swindled in their land purchases; that yellow fever and cholera prevailed, &c. Reports have gone abroad so detrimental that foreign authorities have published warnings not to come to West Virginia or South.—Now, Mr. Editor, I claim that this matter is of such importance that the best and most influential citizens should awaken to its consideration, irrespective of party politics; for I claim that every citizen, be he Democrat, Republican or Greenbacker, is interested in the welfare of the State and her honor. Such charges rest alike upon all of the people of the State, no matter what their political principles may be.

The facts in regard to our Swiss

people are, that instead of their being only one family, there are over thirty in the Kanawha Valley, fifty persons above Cannelton to our knowledge, several families in Kanawha county, also in Cabell county, some 500 persons in Randolph county, a large number in Ohio and Wood counties, besides being scattered over the entire State. Every family that I have heard from that has purchased and located in this State, came to work and by their own industry to secure the comforts of life has succeeded, and is pleased, contented and happy.

Mr. David Braun, the party who is alluded to in that false article as being the person lynched, has written a stirring reply direct to the Berner Post, in which he speaks in the highest manner of the kind, neighborly manner that he has been treated by Southern people. He stated that his wife does work and she takes pleasure in working. He states that the climate is healthy, the soil very productive, though hilly, and is just the country for Swiss mountain people. He indignantly denies all the charges of lynching, &c., and as we are writing these lines, he is awaiting the arrival of a number of his friends and neighbors from Switzerland, who will locate in his neighborhood on Loup Creek, by reason of the pleasing accounts he has given of West Virginia. Mr. Braun is a dead man according to the version of the Anziger des Westes. We will give a brief history of his career here. He left Switzerland with a family of nine, on December 2d, 1879, with the undersigned, and on December 22d arrived at Cotton Hill, Fayette county. He rented a farm and then had barely enough means to provide for the supplies of his family. On November 1, 1880, he was the possessor of a fine horse, a cow, several sheep and hogs, all manner of poultry, had a good crop of oats, corn, vegetables of all kinds, and 30,000 tobacco plants, and he has now two large barns full of as fine cured yellow leaf tobacco as has been raised in that section; and if last year's prices hold good his tobacco crop is worth from $1,000 to $1,500. Though he was lynched as the Anziger will have it, he is to-day the proudest, happiest little live Swiss in America. We doubt if the Anziger, in all the West can show one Swiss or any other new settler without any means who has had a better result from his own labor than Mr. Braun.

Mr. Kirchhoff has traveled all over Switzerland, and in every prominent place has succeeded in contradicting the misrepresentations. He has worked nobly and hard and has a large number of families secured for West Virginia.

Mr. Paul Schink, a young gentleman of true worth, well educated, who is not ashamed of honest toil, desires to make the occupation of a farmer his sphere of life, whose father now is a member of the National Executive Council of Switzerland, and been four different times the President of that body. He has not only written home, but to prominent German papers here, denying the allegations made against our State, and showing up its great advantages. He, with us, is satisfied that no section of America is so well adapted to our Swiss mountain people, taking everything into consideration, as the State of West Virginia.

If this is acceptable, in our next we will treat on other interesting points made by the Anziger and reflection cast by it on our good people of Charleston and our State officials.

Em. D. Ludwig.
